lead: A compound thick cylinder is two or more tubes shrunk one onto the other. A single thick cylinder under internal pressure is worst at the bore, where hoop stress peaks, while outer layers do little work. Shrinking an outer tube on leaves compressive residual hoop stress at the bore, cancelling part of the pressure stress. Gun barrels, hydraulic press cylinders and high-pressure vessels use this. Only a few universities teach this topic.
prereq: You need 7.7 for Lamé's equations, constants A and B, and the sign convention for radial stress.

blocks.text: The inner tube's outside diameter is slightly larger than the outer tube's bore. The difference is the shrinkage allowance. Heat the outer tube until it expands, slip it over, and cool it. On cooling it grips, and a shrinkage pressure p<sub>s</sub> appears at the common surface.

That pressure holds the joint. It pushes radially outward on the inner tube and inward on the outer tube: same pressure, opposite directions. Each tube then carries its own Lamé field with p<sub>s</sub> as its only boundary load. This is the residual field, present before working pressure.

items: Fix the shrinkage allowance and find p<sub>s</sub> from it: the outer tube's bore opens out and the inner tube's outside is squeezed down; these two radial deflections together equal the allowance.
Residual hoop stress at the bore of the inner tube is compressive, written with a minus sign.
Residual hoop stress at the bore of the outer tube is tensile, written with a plus sign.

blocks.text: Run Lamé's equations again for working internal pressure p alone, with zero pressure outside. Add this field to the residual field at the same radius, using the same sign convention: σ<sub>r</sub> is negative when compressive.

blocks.where: σ<sub>θ</sub> is the hoop stress at radius r, in N/m² (Pa); r is the radius in metres. The two hoop stresses are added algebraically at the same point using the same sign convention, so a compressive (negative) residual reduces a tensile (positive) pressure stress.

blocks.text: The gain: at the bore the shrink-fit compression is subtracted from the pressure tension, so peak stress drops and the same wall carries more pressure. Autofrettage does the same by over-pressurising the bore once, so the metal there yields and stays in compression.

blocks.where: σ<sub>r</sub> is radial stress, σ<sub>θ</sub> is hoop stress in any tangential direction, both in Pa; r is the radius in m; A has units of Pa and B of Pa·m³.

blocks.text: The constants come from the two surfaces: σr = −p at the bore r = ri, and σr = 0 at the outside r = ro. Two equations, two unknowns. A sphere carries the same hoop stress in every direction, so it is stronger than a cylinder of the same size, as in 7.6. A compound sphere is analysed the same way: residual field from the shrink fit, pressure field from the load, then add.

figure.caption: The tubes are shrunk together, the fit leaves the bore in compression, and pressure stresses are added to give a lower bore stress.

spec.title: How a compound cylinder is built
spec.aria: Flowchart: inner tube and outer tube are shrink fitted, leaving residual hoop stress, and working pressure stress is added to give a lower bore stress.

examples.question: A compound cylinder is made from two tubes shrunk together. The shrink fit alone leaves a residual hoop stress of −45 MPa at the bore of the inner tube and +45 MPa at the bore of the outer tube. The working pressure alone would give a hoop stress of 120 MPa at the bore of the inner tube. Find the final hoop stress at the bore of the inner tube and the percentage reduction.
steps: Write the superposition: σ<sub>θ,final</sub> = σ<sub>θ,pressure</sub> + σ<sub>θ,residual</sub>.
Substitute at the inner bore: σ<sub>θ,final</sub> = 120 MPa + (−45 MPa).
Reduction = 45 MPa. As a fraction of the pressure-only value: 45/120 = 0.375, that is 37.5 per cent.
examples.answer: The final hoop stress at the bore of the inner tube is 75 MPa (tension), a reduction of 45 MPa, or 37.5 per cent of the pressure-only value.
examples.check:
residual = -45.0
pressure = 120.0
final = pressure + residual
reduction = -residual
fraction = reduction / pressure
print(final)
print(reduction)
print(fraction)

traps: Adding residual and pressure stresses with the wrong signs; the residual at the inner bore is negative and must be subtracted.
Forgetting that shrinkage pressure pushes outward on the inner tube but inward on the outer tube, so the two bores get opposite residual hoop stresses.
Using working pressure where shrinkage pressure belongs, or the reverse, when computing p<sub>s</sub>.
Mixing diameters and radii inside B/r² or B/r³; B changes value if you switch, so stay consistent.
Believing a compound cylinder is just a thick cylinder of the same total wall thickness; the shrink fit is the whole point.

quiz.q: Define the shrinkage allowance in a compound cylinder.
quiz.a: The difference between the outside diameter of the inner tube and the bore diameter of the outer tube, before assembly.

quiz.q: Why does the shrinkage pressure leave the inner bore in compression and the outer bore in tension?
quiz.a: The pressure acts radially outward on the inner tube, so its circumference tries to shrink and the hoop stress is compressive; it acts inward on the outer tube, which is stretched over the inner one, so its hoop stress is tensile.

quiz.q: State the two boundary conditions used to find A and B for a thick sphere under internal pressure p.
quiz.a: σ<sub>r</sub> = −p at r = r<sub>i</sub>, and σ<sub>r</sub> = 0 at r = r<sub>o</sub>.

quiz.q: A compound cylinder has a residual bore hoop stress of −30 MPa and a pressure-only bore hoop stress of 90 MPa. Find the final bore hoop stress.
quiz.a: σ<sub>θ</sub> = 90 + (−30) = 60 MPa, tension. The shrink fit removed one third of the pressure stress.

quiz.q: The same cylinder (residual −30 MPa) must keep the bore hoop stress at or below 100 MPa. What is the largest pressure-only bore hoop stress allowed?
quiz.a: 100 = σ<sub>pressure</sub> − 30, so σ<sub>pressure</sub> = 130 MPa. The shrink fit allows 30 MPa more than a plain cylinder with the same limit.

quiz.q: A plain thick cylinder and a two-tube compound cylinder have the same bore, outside diameter and material. Explain in one line which carries more pressure before yielding at the bore.
quiz.a: The compound one, because the compressive residual hoop stress at the bore cancels part of the tensile pressure hoop stress, so the bore reaches yield at a higher working pressure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gun barrels and autofrettaged fuel-injection lines use this residual-stress trick, and modern vessels sometimes use three or more shrunk layers. Autofrettage is designed by checking where the bore stress first reaches yield and how far the plastic zone spreads. Search for shrink-fit interference pressure, Lamé superposition and autofrettage residual stress if you want the design side.
